customer script adapter and expected inputs/outputs
streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs and SLA targets

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-30 15:00 PDT | Duration: 72m | Attendees: Jesse Kim, Marco Ruiz (Redwood) — Priya Nair, Liam O'Connor, Daniel Chen (AtlasFleet)

Summary (auto): Quick intro, scope POC: mirror live traffic to Redwood harness, validate throughput and latency under AtlasFleet scripts, agree on success criteria and handoffs.

00:00 Jesse Kim: hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time, i'll briefly run through agenda — intro, current infra, target metrics, harness integration, next steps.
00:18 Priya Nair: thanks jesse, quick context — AtlasFleet is running a customer-facing routing assistant, ~120k users nightly, peak windows 18:00-20:00 UTC. we're interested in mirroring traffic to Redwood to validate streaming fallthrough and to compare cost/latency vs our existing setup.
00:37 Marco Ruiz: cool, just to clarify, when you say mirroring do you mean a passive tap where requests are duplicated to the harness or are you looking for a split where a percentage is live routed?
00:49 Liam O'Connor: mostly passive mirror to start — we don't want user-facing differences. we'll provide a copy of the request payloads, sanitized. if the mirror looks good we'll propose a 1% live split later.
01:05 Jesse Kim: perfect. on Redwood side we'll run the harness adapter that consumes your script, we support streaming and non-streaming modes — streaming means partial tokens returned as they generate, non-streaming is full-response after completion.
01:20 Daniel Chen: can you remind us the tradeoffs? latency/story? we've got some stateful context and KV cache concerns.
01:28 Marco Ruiz: sure. streaming typically gives lower perceived latency for users because partial tokens come faster, but throughput inefficiencies can surface if your clients expect fully-structured JSON at the end. with streaming we still measure end-to-end p95 token latency, and we watch token/sec and per-request tail. non-streaming typically has better batching and token efficiency but higher initial latency. also, KV cache warmup — i keep saying K-V cash during notes — our runtime uses a KV cache per session; if the trace has many cold sessions you'll see initial token penalties.
02:05 Priya Nair: our distribution: avg tokens per request ~140, median 110, 95th 420, and we'd expect bursts up to 220 qps for sustained 5–10 min windows.
02:21 Jesse Kim: good, that's helpful. success criteria — what would you call a win post-POC?
02:29 Liam O'Connor: two things: parity for latency (p95 within 1.5x our baseline), and throughput feasibility at target burst without thundering cold-start failures. cost-per-token is secondary but we'd like a ballpark.
02:40 Marco Ruiz: i propose the POC success criteria: 1) p95 streaming under 350ms for interactive flows, or p95 non-streaming end-to-end within 1.5x baseline; 2) handle 220 qps sustained for 10m with <3% error rate; 3) KV cache warmup strategy demonstrates recovery to steady-state within 3 minutes; 4) harness correctly executes your customer scripts with no parsing errors.
03:05 Daniel Chen: sounds reasonable. what about quantization/precision? we use a mix of instruction prompt templates — do you have model variants?
03:14 Marco Ruiz: we will run a compatible open model (we'll propose redwood-curated model IDs in the harness manifest). quantization profiles are on the table; we can show perf delta between float16 and int8-style quant on a small subset. for POC we'll stick to the default recommended quant to reduce noise.
03:35 Priya Nair: security — we need SOC2 attestation and a KMS integration for keys used during the on-prem test. also audit logging retention and RBAC.
03:46 Jesse Kim: yes, we'll send the SOC2 + ISO summary. for KMS we support customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS) for private deployments; for the hosted harness we'll send our KMS integration guide. audit logs are emitted to S3 and can be forwarded to your SIEM.
04:02 Liam O'Connor: great. on harness: how do we feed our scripts? are there adapters?
04:10 Marco Ruiz: the harness adapter expects a JSONL with input records and an adapter shim — we'll provide a small sample repo: github.com/redwood/harness-adapter (placeholder). the adapter can run in streaming mode by default. small differences in the script (like expecting incremental function-calls) can cause parsing errors, so we want to run a quick validate pass on a 1000-record sample.
04:40 Daniel Chen: okay, can your harness simulate KV cache warmup e.g., synthetic pre-warms?
04:47 Marco Ruiz: yes. we can run a warmup phase that replays representative session prefixes to populate the KV cache, or run the mirror in 'learn' mode where mirrored traffic seeds the cache for the live split later. both are supported; we'll coordinate which approach for this POC.
05:10 Jesse Kim: ops questions — network and on-prem footprint. For the on-prem smoke test we need either an outbound TLS endpoint (for hosted harness) or we'll ship a private bundle for air-gapped testing. what does AtlasFleet prefer?
05:25 Priya Nair: security prefers on-prem bundle for the smoke test window; we can stand up a controlled VM in our lab cluster.
05:33 Marco Ruiz: noted. we'll prepare an on-prem bundle with a small runtime, plus deployment instructions. also we need to confirm the CPU/GPU footprint — for the test we can run on a single A100-equivalent instance or a high-memory CPU fallback depending on model size. we'll propose the exact distro after we pick the model variant.
06:00 Liam O'Connor: metrics — what do you need us to provide?
06:05 Jesse Kim: token distribution CSV plus an exemplar traffic capture (sanitized) and your current p95 baseline numbers for the same traffic window. also define SLO gates (e.g., p95 <= X ms, errors <= Y%).
06:18 Priya Nair: we'll provide that by next week.
06:22 Marco Ruiz: timeline proposal: week 1 (this week) — share scripts + trace; week 2 — Redwood runs harness locally against sample offline dataset; week 3 — mirror live traffic for 2 hours during off-peak; week 4 — on-prem smoke test + deep dive; week 5 — results review and decision. does that align?
06:44 Daniel Chen: sounds tight but ok. we may need to push the on-prem smoke test depending on infra team bandwidth.
06:51 Jesse Kim: flexible. we'll keep milestones and define a hard cutover only when you give the go.
06:58 Liam O'Connor: any blockers on the Redwood side?
07:02 Marco Ruiz: main blocker is getting the traffic sample and a sanitized PR with the script semantics. the harness validation pass is quick — usually a few hours. the on-prem bundle needs a signed NDA if you prefer the binary package.
07:20 Priya Nair: we have a standing NDA with Redwood legal, should cover shipping the bundle. i'll confirm this afternoon.
07:29 Jesse Kim: perfect. any other technical concerns?
07:33 Daniel Chen: one small thing — when we mirror do you plan to send back responses to our network or just collect metrics? we might want a passive-only mode that never replies.
07:43 Marco Ruiz: for the POC we'll use passive mode: harness ingests duplicated requests, responds to local harness only, and emits metrics/logs. only when you opt-in to live split do we return to users.
07:55 Jesse Kim: ok let's recap next steps: marco will send harness adapter README + example scripts; jesse will send SOC2/ISO + KMS note; priya will share sanitized traces and confirm NDA; marco and jesse to propose two on-prem test windows.
08:12 Priya Nair: thanks team, excited to see results — especially how the streaming path performs for our assistant.
08:20 Liam O'Connor: quick Q: do you have any tooling to compare output quality between models?
08:25 Marco Ruiz: we have a lightweight eval harness to compute Rouge/BLEU-ish and custom hallucination checks tied to prompt sets; we'll run a small quality eval but the POC scope here is mainly performance and compatibility.
08:40 Jesse Kim: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifact links and schedule.
08:45 (meeting ends)
